description: We’re tackling “Dancing with the SARs,” using NASA-ISRO’s NISAR radar data to track how Earth’s surface shifts: subsidence, landslides, floods, glacier flow. Radar sees through clouds and at night. Our goal is an interactive map or early-warning tool that communities can actually use. Beginners are welcome, and we’ll split the work so everyone builds something real.
summary:
SARtale is a project that helps people watch glacial lakes in the Himalayas and spot when they may be getting dangerous. It uses radar satellite data from NASA’s NISAR mission, which can “see through clouds” and at night, to monitor lake size and change over time. The app checks many lakes in Gilgit-Baltistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and shows whether each one is stable, growing, frozen, or may need attention.

It turns complicated satellite measurements into a clear, easy dashboard for local officials and the public. Instead of reading raw science data, users see a status for each lake, like “alert: growing” or “no lake now,” along with reasons and evidence. This helps people understand which lakes may need closer monitoring or action, especially when cloud cover makes normal optical satellite images hard to use.
details:
SARtale: monitoring glacial lakes through cloud

SARtale is a website and data-processing project that helps people monitor glacial lakes in northern Pakistan. It turns satellite measurements into a clear, lake-by-lake view of changes that may deserve closer attention. It is designed as a screening and information tool—not a flood forecast or official warning system.

What the project does and how it works

The project focuses on glacial lakes in Gilgit-Baltistan and upper Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. These lakes can change over time, but persistent cloud cover can make it hard to observe them with ordinary optical satellite images. SARtale addresses that problem by using NISAR radar imagery, which can collect useful observations through cloud and at night.

Its processing pipeline broadly works as follows:

  1. Find satellite passes: SARtale searches NASA’s catalogue for NISAR radar observations covering each registered lake.
  2. Read the relevant data: It retrieves a small window around each lake, rather than downloading a whole satellite file.
  3. Estimate water area: It processes the radar signal to identify pixels that may represent water and estimates the area within each lake’s mapped outline or search zone.
  4. Compare observations over time: It compares a pass with earlier observations from the same satellite track, accounting for normal variation and measurement noise. This matters because a lake can look different from different viewing angles.
  5. Check the result: Where suitable clear imagery is available, SARtale compares its radar-based water estimate with optical water estimates from Sentinel-2.
  6. Present the results: The website shows each lake’s status, the reason for it, charts, images and other evidence.

The statuses include messages such as “Alert: growing”, “Watch”, “Decrease noted” “Frozen”, “No change”, and “Not measured”. These are intended to communicate what the available observations show, along with reasons and limitations—not to claim certainty about what will happen next.

Benefits and intended impact

Satellite products and statistical methods can be difficult for non-specialists to interpret. SARtale’s main benefit is that it presents the results in one place and in more accessible terms. Users can sort and filter lakes, open a lake’s page to see its evidence, and print a one-page brief.

The intended impact is to help local officials, disaster-management teams, researchers and the public see which lakes may warrant closer review, including during periods when cloud limits optical monitoring. The site also offers a way to request additional lakes for consideration.

SARtale does not replace field observations, expert assessment or official alerts. It screens for slower changes in lake area; it cannot provide reliable advance warning of a sudden outburst, which can unfold much faster than the satellite observation and processing cycle.

Tools and technology

The project combines a Python data pipeline with a static web application:

  • Data processing: Python 3.12, managed with Conda. The pipeline uses NumPy and SciPy for numerical processing, h5py for reading NISAR files, Rasterio and GDAL for geospatial data, PyProj for coordinate transformations, Pillow for images, and Requests for web data access.
  • Website: TypeScript, built with Vite. MapLibre GL is used for the lake locator map, and uPlot for charts. Vitest and jsdom are used for application testing.
  • Data sources: NASA–ISRO NISAR Level-2 GCOV radar data is the main monitoring source. Sentinel-2 L2A imagery is used for optical comparisons and some ice checks. Copernicus DEM GLO-30 supports elevation and terrain-related processing. NASA POWER temperature data also contributes to the freeze check.
  • Hosting and automation: The repository describes publishing the website with GitHub Pages and using GitHub Actions for deployment and data-refresh workflows.
  • Hardware: The project is software-based and does not require custom or specialized hardware. Rebuilding the data pipeline requires an internet connection and NASA Earthdata login credentials for the NASA archive; the website itself reads the prepared data files.

What makes the project creative

SARtale combines radar observations—which are useful when clouds obscure the ground—with optical satellite imagery that can help check those observations when the sky is clear. Rather than presenting raw imagery alone, it turns multiple passes into a history for each lake and communicates the results through plain-language statuses, visual evidence and a guided story.

It also makes its reasoning visible: users can see why a lake received a status and when the data could not support a reliable measurement. The project is not based on an AI prediction model; its method uses documented image-processing and statistical rules.

Factors the team considered

The team considered both the practical challenges of monitoring lakes and the risk of overstating what the data can tell us:

  • Cloud cover: Optical imagery can be unavailable or obscured, so radar is important—but optical data remains useful for cross-checking when it is clear.
  • Measurement uncertainty: Radar images contain noise, and different satellite tracks have different viewing angles. SARtale compares observations against a lake’s own past measurements and filters out some anomalous or insufficiently visible passes.
  • Independent checks: Radar-derived water estimates are compared with Sentinel-2 estimates when a suitably clear, close-in-time scene is available. If validation is missing or poor, the app can limit what it claims.
  • Ice and seasonality: Radar alone cannot reliably distinguish open water from some frozen conditions. SARtale therefore uses temperature and Sentinel-2 evidence in its freeze check, and handles frozen periods separately.
  • Limits of the method: Small lakes, wet shorelines, terrain effects, incomplete outlines and limited observations can affect measurements. The project documents these limitations.
  • Time and safety: Satellite observations do not happen continuously, and processing takes time. SARtale is meant for slow-change screening, not rapid outburst alerts.
  • Who needs to use the information: The team designed the interface to make results easier to scan and understand, with filters, lake-specific evidence and printable summaries.

For the project’s technical method and source details, see the data sources and licences, and repository.
